issues.issue: The Network Operator warrants that "this Agreement constitutes a legal, valid and binding obligation" as of the Effective Date, while Section 12.14 provides the Agreement "shall become binding only upon condition" that the parent delivers an acceptable guaranty. The two cannot both be true at signature.

This is a warranty of historical facts "at all times since January 1, 2005," yet the chapeau of Section 5.1 makes every warranty speak "as of the Effective Date and continuing throughout the Term." A past-fact representation cannot sensibly be made continuing, and it extends to a non-party parent company.

The warranty of having "successfully provided and performed the Services or services that are substantially equivalent ... in other settings and circumstances" has no benchmark for success or equivalence. Whether it was breached cannot be tested against any stated measure.

Performance is warranted to meet "generally accepted industry standards," while Section 4.13.1 measures the same Services against the standards of an SLA that is not yet written. Which standard governs a performance failure is unresolved.

Network Operator warrants it holds all approvals applicable to "the operation of the MTC Network," a network MTC owns and for which MTC and MassDOT hold the underlying property and highway rights. Which authorizations are the operator's responsibility is not delimited.

The covenant to cooperate "to effect the goals, objectives and purposes of this Agreement" in a "commercially reasonable manner" states no ascertainable duty. It could be invoked to require conduct nowhere else specified.

The covenant against any transaction that "would constitute self-dealing" leaves that term undefined, while Section 4.8 expressly contemplates the operator contracting with its own Affiliate and Section 2.43 deems fees on its own extensions. What is prohibited self-dealing and what is permitted Affiliate dealing is not drawn.

Compliance is promised with "Article 5 of the Master Services Agreement between MTC and EOPSS and ITD," a document the same sentence admits is "currently being negotiated." The content of the obligation does not exist at signature.

The operator represents as of the Effective Date that it "has taken out all insurance required under this Agreement," but Section 10.3.3 allows thirty days after the Effective Date for certificates and permits certain coverages to be procured later with MTC's consent. The representation and the insurance timetable do not match.

The operator must "ensure that the MTC Network is and remains" compliant with all laws and Network Policies — an absolute guarantee about an asset MTC owns, designs and builds under Section 4.2.1. The warranty is broader than the operator's control of the subject matter.

Notice must be given "immediately" of any event rendering the warranties incorrect, without a defined period, and several of those warranties (such as Section 5.1.5) are historical facts that no later event can render incorrect. The trigger and timing of the notice duty are both indeterminate.

MTC warrants the Agreement is a binding obligation "as of the Effective Date," while Section 12.14 makes the Agreement binding only on delivery of an acceptable parent guaranty. The warranty and the condition precedent are inconsistent.

The IPT is given the purpose "to resolve disputes submitted by the Parties pursuant to ARTICLE 11," but under Section 11.1.2 the IPT is merely a fifteen-day way station before escalation and arbitration and has no power to decide anything. The resolution function stated here has no counterpart in Article 11.

The IPT includes "one person representing jointly EOPSS and ITD," who is not a representative of either Party, yet Section 11.1.3 lets the IPT stay the arbitration timetable "upon unanimous vote of its members." That gives a non-party a veto over the Parties' dispute resolution clock.

The IPT need "meet at least once a year," while Section 11.1.1.2 requires it to meet "as often as necessary" and Section 11.1.2 gives it only fifteen days to resolve a submitted dispute. The standing meeting obligation does not support the dispute function assigned to it.

Where IPT recommendations are material the Parties "may either negotiate to amend the Agreement ... or consider the change during any subsequent renewal," which obliges neither Party to do anything, yet Section 4.7.5.2 allows the Price Caps themselves to be updated annually with MTC's approval alone. The two routes to changing pricing cannot both be the governing one.

Either Party may demand "at any time" that all Confidential Information be "promptly deliver[ed]" back, which would strip the Network Operator of information the same sentence licenses it to hold "as required to perform the Services." The return right and the performance licence collide within the section.

This subordinates confidentiality to the Public Records Act and to compulsory process, while Section 2.9 and Section 7.1 declare the same material to be the exclusive property of the disclosing party. What protection Confidential Information actually enjoys in MTC's hands is left to Exhibits H-1 and H-2 and to statute.

Network Operator must comply with MTC's confidentiality policies "as communicated by MTC's Executive Director or General Counsel to Network Operator from time to time," which lets MTC add obligations unilaterally, whereas Section 12.1 permits modifications only by a document signed by both Parties. The two provisions cannot both govern later-communicated policies.

The exception turns on direction "by the General Counsel," a person identified nowhere in the Agreement's definitions, and the prohibition runs in favour of "any Person" — another undefined capitalized term. Who must authorize a disclosure is not fixed by the text.

The clause bars use for the benefit of "any Person related to or that is an Affiliate of with Network Operator" — a garbled phrase — and protects "any Applicable Third Party," a capitalized term the Agreement never defines. Both the class of prohibited beneficiaries and the class of protected persons are unascertainable.

The section requires delivery of "all copies of MTC's Written Materials," a capitalized term defined nowhere, and imposes indemnity "to the maximum extent required by law," which is not the usual "permitted by law" and has no evident meaning. Both the property to be returned and the extent of the indemnity are uncertain.

The Parties must cooperate on any statement "relating to or bearing on the work performed or data collected under this Agreement," a scope broad enough to capture routine customer communications, subject only to a carve-out for regulatory reporting. The boundary of the approval requirement is not drawn.

The exceptions are expressed to qualify only "Network Operator's obligations under Section 7.3," leaving the ownership and return obligations in Section 7.1 and the Exhibit H obligations in Section 7.2 without any public-domain or compelled-disclosure carve-out. Whether the carve-outs extend to the rest of Article 7 is open.

Article 8 nowhere uses or defines termination "for cause," yet Sections 3.6.1 and 3.6.2 make the Network Operator's entire Dark Fiber Rights turn on whether "MTC terminates this Agreement for cause." Which of the grounds in 8.1.1 through 8.1.4 count as cause is not stated.

The deferral charge escalates for each thirty-day period "beyond the initial thirty (30) days that the breach remains uncured," but Sections 8.1.2 and 8.1.3 supply no notice-and-cure period at all, so the formula has no starting point for those grounds. The charge cannot be computed for the very breaches it is said to cover.

Termination requires "a disruption to the basic functioning of more than fifty percent (50%) of the MTC Network," without saying whether the fifty percent is measured in route miles, strands, CAIs, customers or revenue. The threshold cannot be applied as written.

Force majeure relief is available only for an event occurring "after the Commencement Date," leaving the operator with no excuse for a Force Majeure Event during the up to thirty months of pre-Commencement obligations imposed by Sections 4.1.10, 4.2.3 and 4.9.4. The gap is created by the section's own words.

"Neither the Term ... nor Network Operator's obligations ... shall be deemed to have expired or terminated until the services transfer assistance ... is completed or MTC waives the requirement," which cannot be squared with Section 3.1's fixed termination on the tenth anniversary of the Commencement Date or with the definition of Term in Section 2.63. On its face it lets MTC extend the operator's obligations indefinitely.

The duty to provide transfer assistance for up to twelve months before expiration, or on any notice of termination, says nothing about who bears its cost or what the assistance consists of beyond "as described herein." Neither the content nor the compensation of the obligation is fixed.

"Upon request by MTC, the effective date of such expiration or termination shall be extended for up to one year" gives MTC a unilateral extension power, whereas Section 3.2 permits extension only "by mutual agreement of the parties" for defined Renewal Terms. The two mechanisms for prolonging the relationship conflict.

Third party agreements are transferred at termination only "on mutually acceptable terms and conditions" and at MTC's request, while Section 4.7.3 effects an immediate present assignment of Third Party Service Provider contracts effective on termination. The same contracts are dealt with by two inconsistent mechanisms.

Network Operator may terminate for MTC's material breach or insolvency, but Section 3.6.1 grants the Dark Fiber Rights only "upon expiration of the Term" and Section 3.6.2 addresses only MTC's for-cause termination. What becomes of the operator's option after its own rightful termination is unaddressed.

The indemnity is limited to the five enumerated categories (a)–(e), which cover third party claims and non-compliance but not the operator's own breach of this Agreement, so whether MTC's direct losses are indemnified turns on the closed list. The enumeration and the opening words "all claims, liabilities, costs, or expenses arising out of" pull in different directions.

The Indemnifying Party controls the defence only "so long as [it] is not in default in the performance of its obligations under the Agreement," without limiting that to material or related defaults. Any alleged default could be used to strip control of the defence.

Any settlement requires "the written approval of both the Parties," which cannot be squared with Section 9.3's grant to the Indemnifying Party of "primary responsibility for the conduct of an Indemnified Claim Proceeding and the defense." Neither section says what happens when approval is refused.

The contractual liability coverage is required to cover "any insurable indemnity obligations under Section 9.1(a), 9.1(d) or 9.1(e)," pointedly omitting 9.1(b) and 9.1(c), while the opening words add "such other coverages as the Parties may determine are commercially reasonable." Whether the omission of two indemnity heads is deliberate is a question the clause invites.

The property coverage the operator must buy is whatever the Parties later "confer" and use "commercially reasonable efforts to agree" upon, with no default level, type or limit if they do not agree. The core property insurance obligation is an agreement to agree.

Earth movement coverage must apply "regardless of any other cause or event contributing concurrently or in any other sequence of Losses," using a capitalized "Losses" that is defined nowhere in the Agreement. The intended anti-concurrent-causation effect is expressed through an undefined term.

The aggregate limit requirement applies only "where possible" and must be "commensurate with the value of the assets in service, or such other value as MTC may approve," which fixes no number and no method. Whether a given limit complies cannot be determined from the text.

Coverage for MTC property in transit or storage is required only "within limits reasonably determined by Network Operator and MTC," leaving the limits to later agreement with no fallback. The obligation is incomplete on its face.

The rental loss cover is required only "subject to such further determination as to commercially reasonable amounts, timing, deductibles, and terms," while Section 2.45 already counts its proceeds as Network Revenue owed in part to MTC. Whether any rental loss cover is actually mandatory is left to a later determination that may never occur.

Network Operator "waives all rights to recover against MTC" for insured loss or damage to its property, which sits against MTC's indemnity of the operator in Section 9.2 for MTC's own contract breaches and legal non-compliance. Whether the waiver defeats an otherwise indemnified claim is unresolved.

The section allows that "certain types of insurance are not required within thirty (30) days of the Effective Date" without identifying which, and requires certificates "within five (5) days of requiring such insurance" — a phrase that does not say what triggers the requirement. Compliance is a condition whose scope cannot be determined, and breach carries a ten-day termination right under Section 8.1.1.

MTC "shall be named as loss payee as its interest may appear on the property insurance policies," while Section 4.11.8.1 requires Network Operator to prosecute the property claims and apply the proceeds itself, subject to MTC approval only above $500,000. Who receives and controls insurance proceeds is answered differently in the two sections.

The additional insurance obligation is measured by "agreements between MTC and others that are within the scope of Section 4.1," but Section 4.1 is a general overview of the operator's responsibilities and identifies no agreements; the third party agreements are dealt with in Section 4.9.2. The cross-reference does not identify the agreements it invokes.

This makes Article 11 the exclusive route for "any dispute between the Parties," whereas the Guaranty Agreement's Section 4.6 gives MTC an election between AAA arbitration and litigation in Middlesex County and purports to incorporate "all other provisions relating to dispute resolution" from this Agreement. How the mandatory clause here operates alongside the guarantor's elective clause is contestable.

The officers are given until thirty days after receipt of the Dispute Resolution Notice to resolve the dispute, yet Section 11.1.3 permits arbitration only if it is unresolved "within forty-five (45) days after the receipt of the Dispute Resolution Notice." The two provisions leave a fifteen-day gap with no stated status.

The section speaks only of "the decision or award" being final, binding and non-appealable and entered as a judgment, and says nothing about interim, partial or provisional awards, although exhaustion of the escalation steps is excused "in the case of an emergency" without defining one. Whether an interim award compelling continued performance is enforceable in court under this clause is left open.

Either Party may "resort to court action for injunctive relief at any time," which cannot be reconciled with Section 11.1.3's stipulation that arbitration "shall be a condition precedent to any suit, action or proceeding instituted in any court." Whether and when a court may act before the arbitrator does is the question the two provisions leave.

Performance continues during a dispute "unless otherwise directed by MTC," a unilateral power given to one Party over obligations that run both ways, with no equivalent for the Network Operator and no statement of whether MTC may thereby suspend its own duties. The scope of that direction is the operative uncertainty.

The Agreement may be modified "only ... by a written document signed by both Parties," yet Section 4.7.5.2 lets Price Caps be updated annually on MTC's approval and Section 7.3 binds the operator to confidentiality policies "communicated" by MTC from time to time. The integration and no-oral-modification rule cannot be given full effect alongside those provisions.

Excuse for the other Party's fault is limited to "nonmonetary obligations," so the operator's payments remain due even where MTC's delay caused the shortfall, subject only to the narrow relief in Section 4.9.2.8. Whether that section is the exclusive monetary relief is the question left open.

Survival is limited to Articles 9 and 11 and "any other provisions that by their terms cannot be performed prior to the expiration or earlier termination," a formula that does not say whether Section 3.6 (dark fiber rights), Article 7 (post-termination confidentiality) or the seven-year record retention duties survive. The catch-all and the specific list pull against each other.

Interest accrues at "three (3) percentage points above the rediscount rate then charged by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston," a rate no longer published under that name. The reference index may be incapable of ascertainment.

An invalid provision is "deemed to be restated to reflect the Parties' original intentions as nearly as possible," which asks a court to rewrite rather than sever. What the restated term would be is left wholly at large.

The permitted assignees are "another entity of the Commonwealth, a subsidiary of MTC or a special purpose entity," but the notice sentence then speaks of MTC assigning "to an Affiliate," a category not used in the permission and defined differently in Section 2.2. Which assignments are permitted and which require notice do not line up.

"Nothing in this Agreement shall be deemed to confer rights on any person not a Party," yet Section 10.3 requires MassDOT and its bond trustees and mortgagees to be named additional insureds and Section 9.1 extends indemnity to Affiliates, officers and agents. Whether those non-parties may enforce anything is a question the clause creates.

Clause (e) deems email notice given "when received electronically if sent by email and one of the delivery methods in (a) through (d) above," which does not say whether the email or the duplicate delivery fixes the effective date. The date of a notice sent both ways is ambiguous.

The general rule that consents "will not [be] unreasonably withheld" cannot be squared with the numerous provisions committing decisions to MTC's "sole discretion," such as Section 2.7 (revision of the CAI list), Section 4.9.7 and Section 8.2. Whether the reasonableness standard overrides those grants of discretion is unresolved.

The proviso reads "provided, however, that Network Operator shall be subject to any application or access fees," which contradicts the concessive structure of the sentence and appears to omit a negative, and the final sentence assigns the operator sole responsibility for approvals for Alterations "to be done by or on behalf of MTC." As written the allocation of fees and of approval responsibility is self-contradictory.

The Parties must "use all reasonable efforts to limit the rights and obligations of Network Operator" so that it is not a Grant subrecipient, an open-ended licence to curtail the very rights the Agreement confers. Which rights and obligations may be limited on that ground is unstated.

This conditions the Agreement on a parent guaranty "in a form acceptable to MTC, with a limit of liability no less than four million ($4,000,000) U.S. dollars," while the executed Guaranty Agreement is "limited to and capped at" exactly $4,000,000 and relieves the Guarantor of all further obligation once that sum is advanced. Whether the guaranteed performance obligations extend beyond that cap is the question the two documents leave open.
